  4. Under Policy for extensions, paste the policy the guide shows, for example {"serverUrl": "https://pbx.example.org"}. People then only sign in.
  5. Save.

Group Policy (after the Chrome and Edge administrative templates are installed)

  1. Chrome: Computer Configuration → Policies → Administrative Templates → Google → Google Chrome → Extensions → Configure the list of force-installed apps and extensions. Add the install line.
  2. Edge: … → Microsoft Edge → Extensions → Control which extensions are installed silently. Add the same install line.
  3. To fill in the server address, add the values from the guide's registry file under Preferences → Windows Settings → Registry.

Intune

  1. Devices → Configuration → Create → Windows 10 and later → Settings catalog.
  2. Add Edge's Control which extensions are installed silently and Chrome's Configure the list of force-installed apps and extensions, each with the install line.
  3. To fill in the server address, deploy the guide's registry file with a script.

People install it themselves: send them Use the Companion extension. It has the steps for loading the extension by hand from their account page.

Every Veyra update re-signs the extension with the same key. The ID stays the same, and pushed browsers fetch new versions by themselves.

5. Check that it worked

The last step of the guide counts the people signed in to the Companion and shows each recent sign-in with its device. Choose Check again after signing in on the test computer.

If nobody shows up:

  1. On the test computer, open chrome://policy (Edge: edge://policy) and choose Reload policies. Look for ExtensionInstallForcelist. If it is missing, the policy has not reached the browser yet. Check the group or organizational unit.
  2. Open chrome://extensions. The Veyra Companion should be listed as installed by your administrator. If the policy is there but the extension is not, the browser could not download it. Check step 2 (the certificate), and check that the computer can reach the Veyra address.
  3. Click the Veyra icon and sign in.

guides.title: Use the Companion extension
guides.summary: Call from your browser, see who is calling, look people up and listen to voicemail with the Veyra Companion.
guides.html:
The Veyra Companion is a small extension for Chrome and Edge. It puts your phone next to your browser:

  • Call any number with one click. Your desk phone rings first. Pick it up, and Veyra then places the call.
  • See who is calling, in a notification, with Call back for missed calls.
  • Look people up in the directory and call them.
  • Listen to voicemail and see your recent calls.
  • Call a number you see on a web page. Select it, right-click, and choose Call … with Veyra.

Getting it

Your school or company may already have installed it for you. Look for the Veyra icon in the browser toolbar, or in the puzzle-piece menu. If it is there, skip to Signing in.

If it is not there:

  1. In Veyra, open your account and find Connected apps → Get the Veyra Companion extension.
  2. Try Add to Chrome first. If the browser refuses, download veyra-companion.zip and unzip it into a folder you keep. Don't delete the folder afterwards: the browser loads the extension from it.
  3. Type chrome://extensions (Edge: edge://extensions) in the address bar. Turn on Developer mode (top right), choose Load unpacked (top left) and pick the unzipped folder.
  4. Pin the Veyra icon from the puzzle-piece menu so it is always visible.
An extension installed this way does not update itself. When your administrator tells you there is a new version, download the zip again and replace the folder's contents.

Signing in

  1. Click the Veyra icon.
  2. If the server address is not filled in already, enter the address you use for Veyra, for example https://pbx.example.org.
  3. Sign in with your Veyra e-mail and password and your authenticator code. If there is a Sign in with Google (or Microsoft) button, use that instead.

The Companion stays signed in while you use it, and signs out after 30 days without use. Every browser you sign in from is listed on your account under Connected apps. You can sign it out from there, for example if you lose a laptop.

Making a call

  • Type a number in the Companion and choose Call, or pick someone from your favourites, the directory or your recent calls.
  • Your desk phone rings. Pick it up and the call goes out. Outside numbers get the outside-line prefix automatically.
  • If you have more than one extension, choose which phone should ring.

Settings

Right-click the Veyra icon and choose Options for:

  • the outside-line prefix,
  • which notifications you get,
  • Handle phone links, so clicking a tel: link on a web page calls through Veyra instead of opening another app,
  • your speed dials.

Settings are saved to your Veyra account, so they follow you to another computer.

If something doesn't work

  • "Cannot reach the server" or a certificate error: the computer does not trust the Veyra server's certificate. Ask your administrator. They can fix it for everyone.
  • The phone does not ring: check on My Phone that the phone is registered and that Do Not Disturb is off.

guides.title: Updates and maintenance windows
guides.summary: Install new Veyra releases and operating system updates, now or in a maintenance window, from the web page or the server console.

headings.title: What an update does to calls
Install in the maintenance window instead

guides.html:
Open System → Updates. The page has three tabs: Updates (what is available and what was installed), Settings (how each part of the system is updated) and System packages (Ubuntu's own updates).

Veyra releases are signed. Veyra downloads them only from the official Veyra feed, checks the signature, size and checksum, and refuses anything else.

What an update does to calls

  • A Veyra update restarts the web interface and the API, usually for under a minute. Calls are not affected. The database and configuration are backed up first, and if the database step fails the previous version is put back.
  • Operating system packages do not affect calls, except Asterisk (the telephony engine): upgrading it restarts it, which drops calls in progress. That is why Veyra holds Asterisk back unless you include it.

Install a Veyra release now

  1. On the Updates tab, choose Check now (top right) if you do not want to wait for the next automatic check.
  2. In Available updates, choose Review and install on the release. The window shows the release notes, the Service impact, and a list of Checks: the release is newer, it can be installed from your version, your modules support it, there is enough disk space (2 GB plus the release), and no other installation is running. A failed check shows Blocked.
  3. Choose Download and install now. (Or Download and verify only to fetch it now and install later.)

The window then follows the installation live: Approved, Pre-checks passed, upgrade service started, Release verified and unpacked, Installer running (with the installer's output) and Finished. The first stage can take up to a minute, because a background worker starts the upgrade on its next pass. While Veyra restarts, the page says Veyra is restarting; this page reconnects by itself. When it is done, choose Reload the page.

You can close the window at any time; the same progress shows at the top of the page.

Install in the maintenance window instead

Once a release is Downloaded, its review window offers Install in maintenance window (if the Veyra policy has a window) beside Install now. The release then shows Approved · maintenance window and installs in the next window, only when no call is in progress. Withdraw approval cancels it.

Install from the server console

If the web interface is not available, or you prefer the console, run on the server:

sudo veyra updates install

It checks the feed, downloads and verifies the newest release, approves it and starts the installation, exactly as the web page does, and prints each step until it finishes. The web page shows the same progress and history. Useful options:

  • sudo veyra updates install 0.27.44 installs that offered version instead of the newest.
  • --no-wait returns as soon as the installation has started.
  • sudo veyra updates check only checks; it never installs.

The approval is recorded in the audit log as done by cli (<your user name>).

Choose how updates happen

On the Settings tab:

Notifications: Email notifications to lists the addresses told when a release is available, downloaded, installed or failed. Email must be set up under System → Settings → Email delivery.

Update policies: one card per part of the system: Veyra application, Modules, Provisioning templates, Telephony engine (Asterisk) and Operating system. Each card has:

  • Update behaviour:
    • Manual only: nothing happens by itself; an administrator checks and installs.
    • Notify: checks on a schedule and emails; nothing is downloaded or installed.
    • Download, install on approval: downloads new releases; an administrator approves them (Veyra application only).
    • Install automatically in a maintenance window: installs the chosen kinds of update in the window, when no call is in progress. Other releases wait for approval.
  • Release channel: Stable for production. Beta and Development are pre-release software.
  • Check for updates automatically and Check every (hours).
  • Notify administrators.
  • Maintenance window (Veyra, Asterisk and the operating system): turn on Use a maintenance window, tick the days, set Starts at, Length (minutes) (30 to 720) and the Time zone.
  • In automatic mode, what installs by itself: Security, Bug fixes and Features for Veyra; Every update except Asterisk or Security updates only for the operating system; and for Asterisk, Install Asterisk updates in the window when no call is in progress.

Choose Save policy on each card you change.

A common choice for a school or office: Veyra on Install automatically in a maintenance window with Security and Bug fixes ticked, on Saturday at 02:00; the operating system on Security updates only in a Sunday window; Asterisk on Notify.

Operating system packages

The System packages tab lists the Ubuntu packages that can be upgraded, checked daily. Packages marked security fix security problems; restarts Asterisk means the package belongs to the telephony engine.

  • Check now refreshes the list.
  • Install security (n) installs only security updates. Asterisk is upgraded only if it has a security update itself.
  • Install all except Asterisk (n) installs everything else. Calls are not affected.
  • Include Asterisk installs everything. Calls in progress drop and phones re-register. If calls are in progress, Veyra asks again and offers Drop the calls and install.

Progress and output show on the card. A Veyra backup is taken before each run. If the server needs a restart afterwards (for example a new Linux kernel), the card says so. Veyra never restarts the server by itself; do it at a quiet time, because calls drop while it is down.

High availability pairs

On a pair, update the standby first. The page shows Update the standby first with the order: install on the standby (Install … on the standby), switch over to it, install on the old primary, and optionally switch back. See High availability.

Managed by a central console

If this server is enrolled in a central console that sets the update policy, the page shows Managed by the central console, and changes made here are replaced at its next check-in. See Central management of several servers.

When it does not work

  • Last check shows No update source or Failed: read Details. The server must reach the internet over HTTPS.
  • A check says Blocked: the reason is on the line. Low disk space is the most common: free some space on /.
  • The installation failed: the progress shows the error and the installer's output, and the path of the full log on the server. The previous version keeps running.
  • History: the Update history card lists every installation with its result and who started it.

guides.title: Backups and restore
guides.summary: Schedule verified, encrypted backups, copy them to a NAS, an SFTP server or S3 storage, and restore a server from one.
guides.html:
Open System → Backups. Veyra backs up everything needed to rebuild the phone system:

  • the database (extensions, users, call flows, settings, call history),
  • the configuration and secrets, including the keys and certificates phones trust,
  • the telephony engine's configuration,
  • prompts, hold music, firmware, provisioning templates and modules,
  • voicemail,
  • and, if you choose, call recordings.

Every backup is verified before it counts: Veyra restores the database into a scratch database, compares it, and checks every file. A backup that fails verification is kept, marked failed, and raises an alert.

Scheduled backups are on from installation, every day at 02:30 server time.

The summary

Three cards at the top:

  • Last good backup: when the last verified backup was taken. No verified backup in the last two days means something is wrong.
  • Encryption: age when backups are encrypted, Off when they are not.
  • Schedule: the daily time, or Off, and the last error if the last run failed.

Settings

Choose Save after changing any of these.

  • Scheduled backups: on or off.
  • Time of day: server local time, such as 02:30.
  • Keep daily for (days) (default 14), Then one per week for (weeks) (default 8), and Keep pre-upgrade backups (default 3). Old backups are removed only after a new one succeeds.
  • Include call recordings: recordings are usually the largest files. Without them, a restore keeps the list of recordings but not the audio.
  • Encryption recipients (age public keys, one per line): see below.

Turn on encryption

Without encryption, backups stay on the server, readable only by its administrator (root). Before backups leave the server, encrypt them.

Veyra encrypts with age to a public key you give it. Only the matching private key can decrypt, and Veyra never has it.

  1. On a computer that is not the Veyra server, install age and run age-keygen -o veyra-backup-identity.txt. It prints a public key starting with age1….
  2. Paste that public key into Encryption recipients and Save. An SSH public key (ssh-ed25519 …) works too.
  3. Keep veyra-backup-identity.txt safe, in more than one place, such as your password manager or a safe.
Without the private key, an encrypted backup cannot be restored by anyone. Test a restore once, on a spare server, while you still have the original.

Copy backups off the server

A backup that only lives on the server is lost with the server. Under Destinations, choose Add a destination (up to five):

KindWhat you need
FolderA share mounted on the server (NFS or Windows/SMB), for example /mnt/nas/veyra. Mount it in /etc/fstab so it is there after a restart; Veyra does not mount it.
SFTP serverA server reachable over SSH (a NAS with SFTP turned on, a Linux server): its Server name, Port, User name and Folder on the server.
S3-compatible storageAmazon S3, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Cloudflare R2, MinIO and others: the Endpoint (empty for Amazon S3), Region, Bucket, an optional Folder in the bucket, and an Access key ID with its Secret access key.

Set up encryption first (below). Until there is a recipient, the page warns that backups leave the server unencrypted, and they include the configuration's secrets.

SFTP: Veyra signs in with its own SSH key, not a password. The dialog shows the public key: add it to the user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. Then choose Test. The first test shows the server's host key; compare it with what the server shows (ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub as root) and choose This is the server's key. Veyra then refuses any other server at that address.

S3: create an access key that can only list, write and delete in this bucket. The secret is stored encrypted and never shown again; to change it, enter a new one when editing. Most S3-compatible storage needs Path style addressing, which is the default when you enter an endpoint.

How copies work:

  • After each verified backup, Veyra copies every verified backup the destination is missing, newest first, and checks each copy (sizes, and for S3 a checksum of every upload). A copy is written under a temporary name and only takes its real name when it is complete.
  • A copy that fails does not fail the backup. It raises the Backup copy to a destination failed alert, the destination shows last copy failed with the reason, and the next backup copies what is missing.
  • Each destination keeps backups by the same rule as the server unless you turn off Same keep policy as on this server and give it its own, for example a longer history off-site. Old copies are removed there by that rule.
  • Test writes, checks and removes a small file. For a Folder it only checks that the folder exists, because the copies are written by the backup service as root.
  • Remove stops the copies; the copies already made stay where they are.
The Copy to directory setting of earlier releases is now a Folder destination named Copy folder.

Take a backup now

Choose Back up now. A Backup running note shows the current step. Take one before a large change, such as importing many extensions.

The backup list

Each row shows when it was Taken and how (Scheduled, Manual or Before upgrade, which Veyra takes before every update), its State, Size, Contents, whether it is Encrypted (age or clear), the Copies to each destination (name: ok or failed, or local only), and the Veyra Version it came from. Delete removes the files from the server and from every destination.

Backups are stored on the server in /var/backups/veyra.

Restore a server

Restoring is done on the server console, as root, on a server with the same Veyra release installed. A freshly installed server is fine: see Install Veyra.

  1. Copy the backup file (veyra-<date>-<time>.tar.age) and your identity file onto the server.
  2. Run: `` sudo veyra backup restore /var/backups/veyra/<backup>.tar.age --identity ~/veyra-backup-identity.txt `` It asks for confirmation, because it replaces the database, configuration and data of the server.
  3. When it finishes, run sudo installer/verify.sh.

The database, configuration and secrets, engine files, data and voicemail come back; if the backup is from an older release, the database is upgraded; the services restart. Because the server's identity, keys and certificates are in the backup, phones keep trusting it and a central console keeps recognising it.

Other console commands: sudo veyra backup list lists backups and sudo veyra backup run takes one. --parts db,etc,engine,data,voicemail,recordings restores only some parts.

A backup from a newer Veyra release is refused; install that release first. A server that is part of a high availability pair cannot be restored directly; restore a standalone server and build the pair again.

When it does not work

  • Last run failed: the Schedule card shows the error, and the Backup failed alert is raised (see Health, alerts and diagnostics). Disk space is the usual cause.
  • Copy failed: the destination shows the reason. A folder that is not mounted, an SFTP server that refuses Veyra's key (add the public key again) or whose host key changed (confirm the new one with Test if the server was reinstalled), or S3 credentials or a region that are wrong. Fix it and choose Test; the missing copies are made at the next backup.
  • No recent good backup: the No recent good backup alert is raised after two days without a verified backup.

Copy backups to Google Drive

Backups can go to a Shared drive in your Google Workspace. Personal Google accounts and My Drive do not work, because a service account has no storage of its own.

  1. In the Google Cloud console, create a project and enable the Google Drive API.
  2. Create a service account and download a JSON key for it.
  3. Create a Shared drive and add the service account's email address as a Manager.
  4. On this page, add a destination, choose Google Drive, and enter the Shared drive's ID and the contents of the key file.
  5. Choose Test. It writes a file and deletes it for good.
the service account must be a Manager, not a Content manager. A Content manager can only move files to the trash, where they stay for 30 days, so old backups and archived recordings would outlive their deletion. Test fails with that message if the role is wrong.

Archive call recordings

Under Recording archive, choose a destination to keep a copy of every call recording there, in case this server is lost. Copies start within the hour. The first run after turning it on works through your older recordings, up to 500 an hour.

A copy lives exactly as long as its recording. When a recording is deleted, by hand or at its retention date, Veyra deletes its copy too, usually within an hour, and checks that it is gone. If it cannot, it keeps trying and raises an alert. Held recordings and their copies stay.

the archive does not keep recordings longer than your retention period. To keep them longer, lengthen the retention on the recording policy.

A destination that holds copies cannot be removed, because Veyra must be able to delete them. Restoring a copy is not in the interface yet.

guides.title: Deploy changes to the phone system
guides.summary: Send saved changes to the telephony engine, now or when calls have ended, and roll back to an earlier configuration.
guides.html:
When you save a change that affects calls (a new extension, a ring group, a route), it is stored in Veyra's database but the telephony engine (Asterisk) does not use it yet. You deploy it when you are ready. That way you can make several changes and send them together.

The Deploy changes button

While saved changes wait, the top bar shows a red Deploy changes button and a Review link.

  • Deploy changes deploys now.
  • The arrow beside it opens two choices:
    • Deploy now: reloads only the parts of the engine that changed. Calls in progress are not interrupted.
    • Deploy when no calls are active: waits until no call is up, for up to 30 minutes, then deploys anyway. Use it for changes to the SIP transports (ports, TLS), which phones notice.

While it runs the top bar shows Deploying #n, or Waiting for n calls to end (revision #n). When it is done you see Revision #n deployed. Phones will pick up the change. If nothing actually changed, you see Nothing to apply.

If your role cannot deploy, the top bar shows Changes pending deployment instead; ask someone who can.

The button is greyed out when the telephony engine is not running.

Review before deploying

Review opens System → Telephony Engine. The Configuration card shows the Deployed revision, a deployment In progress, and whether there are Pending changes.

Generate configuration builds a new revision from the database without deploying it, so you can see exactly what would change. Each revision is listed under Revisions. Choose View to open one:

  • the changed files with the lines added and removed (files with passwords show contains credentials; diff hidden),
  • All files in this revision,
  • Deploy to send it to the engine now, When no calls are active to wait until no call is up (for up to 30 minutes) and then send it, or Discard to throw it away.

File contents are shown to platform administrators only.

What deploying does

Veyra checks the generated configuration first. A revision with problems shows Failed and is never deployed. When a deployment fails part-way, Veyra puts the previous files back and reloads them, so the engine keeps running the last good configuration. The revision shows Failed with the reason.

Roll back

Every deployed revision is kept. To go back to an earlier configuration:

  1. On System → Telephony Engine, choose View on the older revision (it shows Superseded).
  2. Choose Roll back to this revision. Or choose When no calls are active to roll back once the calls have ended.

The newer revision is marked Rolled back. The database is not changed, so the top bar shows Deploy changes again until you fix or undo the change in Veyra; deploying then sends the database's current state.

Revision states

StateMeaning
Ready to deployGenerated and checked; not sent yet
Deploying…Being written and loaded
DeployedWhat the engine runs now
SupersededRan earlier; a later revision replaced it
Rolled backReplaced by deploying an older one
FailedDid not pass the checks, or could not be loaded

SIP and media settings

The SIP and media settings card on the same page holds the ports and addresses phones and trunks use: the UDP, TCP and TLS ports, the TLS certificate, the RTP port range, the External signaling address and External media address for a server behind NAT, the Local networks, the Default language and the Codecs. Saved settings apply at the next deployment; use Deploy when no calls are active for them.

From the server console

  • sudo veyra config status shows the engine and recent revisions.
  • sudo veyra config generate --deploy generates and deploys.
  • sudo veyra config deploy <number> deploys the revision with that number (such as 42), which is how you roll back from the console. Add --when-idle to wait for calls to end.

When it does not work

  • The engine is not running: see Health, alerts and diagnostics.
  • Installation key missing: the page says so. Revisions with SIP passwords cannot be made without it. Run sudo veyra installation-key check on the server, and restore the key from a backup if it is gone.
  • "The deployer has not reported a result yet": run journalctl -u veyra-deployer on the server.

Custom dialplan

Platform administrators can add their own Asterisk contexts under System → Telephony Engine → Custom dialplan, for something Veyra has no feature for. Contexts must be named [custom-…]. Commands that reach the server's shell or files are refused when you save. Saving does not change calls: deploy the changes as usual.

To send calls there, choose Custom dialplan as the destination of an inbound route, a menu key or anywhere else a call can be sent. Calls start at the context's s extension, so only contexts that have one are listed. Only platform administrators can choose it. A context in use cannot be removed until nothing sends calls to it.

this is code that runs on the server, and it can dial out past classes of service and outbound routes. Only paste dialplan you understand.

guides.title: Import and export with CSV files
guides.summary: Create or change many extensions, users, routes or groups at once with a spreadsheet, or move from FreePBX.
guides.html:
Open System → Import and Export. You can export what exists as a CSV file, change it in a spreadsheet, check it, and import it again. Every row goes through the same checks as the web pages, so a CSV cannot do anything the pages would refuse.

What you can import

Extensions, Users, Ring groups, Queues, IVR menus, Time conditions, Inbound routes and Shared voicemail inboxes.

How the file works

  • The first line names the columns. An export is always a valid import.
  • The first column is the key: extensions, ring groups, queues and shared inboxes by number, users by email, inbound routes by did, IVR menus and time conditions by name. A row whose key exists updates it; otherwise it creates a new one.
  • An empty cell keeps the current value. A dash (-) clears it.
  • Yes/no cells take yes or no. Lists (such as members, pickup_groups or roles) are separated by ;.
  • At most 5,000 rows and 5 MB per file. A key appearing twice is an error.
  • Importing never deletes an extension, user or other item; remove those on their own pages. List columns such as members are the full list, though: a member left out of the list leaves the group.
Import users before the extensions that name them (user_email), and extensions before the groups that list them.

Export or get a template

  1. Under 1. Choose what, pick the Kind (and the Organization, if you have several). The columns are listed below it.
  2. Export … downloads what exists today. Blank template downloads just the header line.

Check, then import

  1. Change the file in a spreadsheet and save it as CSV.
  2. Under 2. Check and import, choose the CSV file.
  3. Choose Check the file. Nothing changes yet. The summary says how many rows would be created, updated, unchanged or have errors, and the Rows table shows each line with Create, Update, No change or Error and the reason.
  4. Fix the errors in the file and check again, or go ahead without them.
  5. Choose Import n rows. Rows with errors are left out and listed.
  6. Use Deploy changes in the top bar to send the changes to the phone system. See Deploy changes to the phone system.

If you can export but not import a kind, the page says You cannot change …: your role lets you see it but not change it.

Moving from FreePBX

The From FreePBX card turns a FreePBX database into the files above. Extensions, ring groups, queues, IVR menus, time conditions and inbound routes come across.

  1. If FreePBX used shorter extensions than Veyra's numbering plan, widen the numbering plan under Settings first.
  2. On the FreePBX server run mysqldump asterisk > asterisk.sql (it may be gzipped).
  3. Choose the file under FreePBX database dump. Optionally add voicemail.conf to keep PINs and emails, and the output of asterisk -rx "database show QPENALTY" saved as a text file to keep queue agents who log in with a code.
  4. Choose Read the FreePBX files. Nothing is saved yet. A list of things to do by hand shows what could not be converted.
  5. Bring the recordings and hold music over: on the FreePBX server run tar czf audio.tar.gz -C /var/lib/asterisk sounds/en/custom moh, choose the file under Audio archive and choose Import the audio. Keep the database dump chosen, so recordings keep the names the IVR menus look for. The archive can be up to 1000 MB. Nothing already in the library is changed, so you can run it again. A list shows anything that could not be read, for example a file over 25 MB or 5 minutes.
  6. Choose each Check n … button in order (extensions, ring groups, queues, IVR menus, time conditions, inbound routes). Each loads the converted file into 2. Check and import; check it and import it before the next.
SIP passwords are not carried over from FreePBX.

guides.title: Health, alerts and diagnostics
guides.summary: See whether everything is running, get emailed when something breaks, and capture SIP traffic or read engine logs to find out why.
guides.html:
Three pages under System help when something is wrong:

  • Health: is everything running right now?
  • Alerts: problems Veyra noticed, and who gets emailed about them.
  • Diagnostics: packet captures, engine logs and engine queries, to find the cause.

System health

System → Health refreshes every 15 seconds.

  • Overall: one status for the whole system, and the Veyra version.
  • Database (PostgreSQL), Telephony engine and Modules: each with its status and details.
  • CPU, Memory, Disk and Uptime of the server.
  • Modules: each installed module with its State and Health.

From the server console, sudo veyra status prints the same summary.

Alerts

System → Alerts lists problems Veyra watches for. The list shows Raised now by default; switch to Cleared or All to see history. Each alert shows what is wrong, since when, when it cleared, and whether its email could be sent.

The rules

RuleRaised when
Telephony engine downAsterisk does not answer
Trunk downA trunk to your phone provider is not registered or not reachable
Veyra service not runningOne of Veyra's background services stopped
Disk space lowFree space falls below the limit (10 % by default)
HTTPS certificate expiringThe web certificate expires within the limit (21 days by default)
Public certificate not renewedA Let's Encrypt renewal failed
Many firewall bansMore bans per hour than the limit (20 by default): probably an attack
Phones unregisteredMore than the limit (20 % by default) of phones are not registered
Backup failed, No recent good backup, Backup copy to a destination failedSee Backups and restore
Instance not checking in, Instance unhealthy, Instance update failedOn a central console only
HA node offline, Replication broken, Replication lagging, File sync failing, Primary isolated, HA operation failedOn a high availability pair only

Who gets told

By default, alerts show only on this page. To email people, click a rule under Rules and set:

  • Enabled.
  • Raise after (minutes): how long the problem must last before anyone is told, so short blips are ignored.
  • Limit, for rules that have one (percent free, days, bans per hour).
  • Email to: one address per line. People are emailed when the alert is raised, every 24 hours while it lasts, and when it clears.

Email must be set up under System → Settings → Email delivery.

Diagnostics

System → Diagnostics has three tabs. Everything here can contain phone numbers, names and, for audio, the content of calls. Downloads, log reads and queries are recorded in the audit log.

Packet captures

A packet capture records the SIP messages between phones, trunks and Veyra, so you can see why a phone does not register or a call fails.

  1. Under Start a capture, choose what to Capture:
    • All SIP: everything on the SIP ports.
    • An extension (where its phone registers from): traffic of that phone. If the phone is not registered, use an address instead.
    • A trunk: traffic to and from your phone provider.
    • An address or network: such as 192.168.1.20 or 10.0.0.0/8.
  2. Set Duration (minutes) (up to 30) and Size limit (MB) (up to 500). The capture stops at whichever comes first.
  3. Tick Include RTP (media) only for audio problems: it records the audio of calls.
  4. Choose Start. Wait until the row shows Running (a few seconds), then reproduce the problem: make the call, restart the phone.
  5. Choose Stop, or let it finish.

Two captures can run at a time.

On a finished capture:

  • SIP shows a readable summary: one row per call or registration (dialog), with who talked to whom and the last answer (such as 200 OK, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found). Click a row to see its messages. For TLS connections the content is encrypted and cannot be read.
  • Download saves a .pcap file that opens in Wireshark. The first time, Veyra reminds you that it is personal data.
  • Delete removes it from the server. Delete captures when you are done.

From the console: sudo veyra capture start --host 192.168.1.20, then list, stop and delete.

Logs

Shows the last lines of the engine's logs: Engine messages (notice, warning, error), Security events (failed registrations, blocked requests) and Queue events. Choose the Log, the number of Lines (up to 2,000), optionally text it must be Containing (such as an extension number), and Show.

Engine queries

A fixed list of read-only questions to Asterisk, such as Every endpoint with its state, Registered contacts, Trunk registrations, Channels and calls up now and Do Not Disturb, forwards and follow-me as the engine has them. One endpoint in full takes an extension number as its Argument. Choose Run.

Common problems

  • A phone does not register: run Registered contacts, then capture the phone's address. A 401 answer again and again means a wrong password; nothing at all means the phone cannot reach the server (check the network and the firewall's bans; see Firewall and bans).
  • Calls have no audio or one-way audio: capture with Include RTP (media), and check the External media address and Local networks in the SIP settings (see Deploy changes to the phone system).
  • A trunk is down: run Trunk registrations and capture the trunk.

guides.title: High availability
guides.summary: Run Veyra on two servers so a standby can take over when the primary needs maintenance or fails.

headings.title: 1. Enable high availability on the first server

guides.html:
With high availability, two Veyra servers work as one phone system. The primary handles calls. The standby keeps a live copy of the database and the files (prompts, voicemail, firmware) and can take over:

  • by a planned switchover, while both servers are up (for maintenance or updates), in about a minute;
  • by a failover, from the standby, when the primary is lost.

Phones and browsers use one service name and service address, which moves to whichever server is primary.

Veyra never fails over by itself. With only two servers, a server cannot tell a dead partner from a broken network cable, and two primaries at once would both take calls and change the database. A person decides. At most one server ever runs the telephony engine, holds the service address and writes the database.

Open System → High Availability. You need to be a platform administrator.

What you need

  • A second server with the same Ubuntu release.
  • Both servers on the same network segment (the same VLAN).
  • A service name (such as veyra.example.org) and a free service address on that segment. The name must point at the address in your DNS.
  • The name of the network interface that will carry the address (such as ens18).

1. Enable high availability on the first server

On a standalone server the page shows Standalone and whether the HA agent is running.

  1. Choose Enable high availability.
  2. Fill in the Service name, Service address, Prefix length (24 for a typical /24 network) and Interface.
  3. Leave Synchronous replication off unless you have a reason (see Options below).
  4. Choose Enable.

The database is reconfigured and restarted once (calls are not affected; the web page reconnects). The HTTPS certificate is reissued for the service name and both server names. Afterwards use the service name to reach Veyra.

2. Add the standby

  1. Choose Add node. Veyra shows a command with a one-time join token. Copy it now: it is shown once and expires in 24 hours. Note the Fingerprint.
  2. On the second server, get the same Veyra release (see Install Veyra) and run the command, from the Veyra folder. It looks like: `` sudo installer/install.sh --role secondary --join https://<primary> --token <token> ``
  3. The installer copies the credentials and certificates, copies the database and starts replication. Asterisk is installed but stays stopped on the standby.

The page now shows both servers. Each card shows its Role, State, Version, Database replication, Replication lag, Last heartbeat, File sync and whether it holds the Service address.

Switch over (planned)

Use this before maintenance on the primary, or to update a pair (see Updates and maintenance windows).

  1. On the primary, choose Switch over to <standby> on the standby's card.
  2. Veyra checks the preconditions: both servers online and on the same version, replication streaming with little lag, file sync fresh, nothing else in progress. If something is wrong it says what, under Not possible now.
  3. Type the standby's name and choose Switch over.
Calls in progress end. Asterisk stops on the old primary and starts on the new one. Phones re-register within their registration time; trunks re-register at once. It takes about a minute.

The progress shows step by step. The old primary becomes the standby.

Fail over (the primary is down)

Do this only when the primary is really down.

  1. Open the standby's own address in the browser (its web page is read-only, but it offers failover).
  2. Choose Fail over to this node. The window shows the primary's last heartbeat and what may be lost: changes after the last replicated moment and files changed since the last sync.
  3. Unless fencing is set up, tick I confirm <primary> is powered off or disconnected. This is recorded in the audit log.
  4. Type FAIL OVER and choose Fail over.

When the old primary comes back, it must not act as primary. Choose Rejoin on its card to make it the new standby.

Fencing (Proxmox)

If both servers are Proxmox virtual machines, Fencing → Configure lets Veyra switch off the old primary's VM before a failover, so you do not have to confirm it by hand. Enter the Proxmox API address, an API token id and API token secret (the token needs VM.PowerMgmt on both VMs), the Proxmox node, the VM id of each server, and the certificate settings. If stopping the VM fails, the failover stops.

An isolated primary

If the primary loses contact with the standby, it stops serving calls (the standby may have taken over) and the page says This primary is isolated. If the standby really is down, choose Resume as primary and type RESUME. If the standby is up, fix the network; the primary rejoins by itself.

Options

On the primary:

  • Replication: Asynchronous (recommended): the primary never waits for the standby, but a failover may lose the last moments of changes. Synchronous: every change waits for the standby, and changes stop entirely while the standby is down; switching back to asynchronous is the way out.
  • Include call recordings in the file sync: recordings are large; without them, recordings made on the old primary are unavailable after a failover until it is back.

Remove the standby

Remove on the standby's card (type its name) takes it out of the pair. That server then refuses to run the telephony engine until sudo veyra ha standalone is run on it. With one server left, the installation is standalone again.

Events and alerts

Events lists switchovers, failovers and role changes. The alerts HA node offline, Replication broken, Replication lagging, File sync failing, Primary isolated and HA operation failed watch the pair (see Health, alerts and diagnostics).

On the console, sudo veyra ha status shows the server's state.

guides.title: Central management of several servers
guides.summary: Watch several Veyra servers from one console, give them shared policies, and send them update commands.
guides.html:
A district or company with several Veyra servers (one per school or site, for example) can watch them all from one place. One Veyra server acts as the central console. The others enroll with it: they report their health every few minutes and accept the policies and commands you choose.

  • The console never connects to the other servers. They check in to it over HTTPS with signed messages, so they can sit behind firewalls.
  • Each server keeps working on its own if the console is unreachable.
  • Each server decides which kinds of policy it accepts.

Two pages are involved:

  • System → Central console on the console server.
  • System → Central management on each managed server.

1. Turn on the console

On the server that will be the console, open System → Central console and switch on Act as a central console. The card shows its Address and Fingerprint, and Minutes without a check-in after which a server counts as offline.

2. Create an enrollment token

  1. On the Enrollment tokens tab, choose New token.
  2. Give it a Label (such as High school; it becomes the server's name on the console) and choose a Policy, or leave it on the default policy.
  3. Copy the Console address, Token and Fingerprint now: the token is shown once. It works once and expires after a day.

3. Enroll the other server

On the server to be managed, open System → Central management:

  1. Under Enroll with a central console, enter the Console address, Enrollment token and Console fingerprint. The fingerprint makes sure you are enrolling with your console and not an impostor.
  2. Only if this server does not trust the console's certificate (for example, the console uses its own Veyra certificate), paste the console's CA certificate (the text of its veyra-ca.crt) under Certificate authority (optional). Not needed when the console has a public certificate.
  3. Choose Enroll.

The page then shows the Console, What this installation accepts, the Policy from the console with the result of each section, and Recent activity. Check in now checks in at once.

Choose what a server accepts

Under What this installation accepts, each of Update policy, Firewall allow list, Alert recipients, Notice banner and Commands from the console can be switched off, keeping it under local control. The console sees what a server refuses.

Watch the servers

On the console, the Instances tab lists every enrolled server with its Status, Last check-in, Version (and any update available), registered Phones, Calls, open Alerts and Policy. Click a server to see more:

  • Status, Telephony and Version at a glance, and a Last 30 days chart of phones, calls and alerts.
  • Open alerts, firewall state, updates waiting and installed modules.
  • Settings here: change its Label and Policy.
  • Commands: what was sent and the result.

The console's own alerts Instance not checking in, Instance unhealthy and Instance update failed tell you when a server needs attention.

Policies

On the Policies tab, New policy (or click one to change it). A policy can set any of these sections; sections you leave off stay under each server's own control:

  • Updates: turn on Set the update policy to set the Mode, a maintenance window, and which kinds of update install automatically. See Updates and maintenance windows. Update email recipients (optional) sets who is told about updates.
  • Firewall: Add addresses to the allow list, one address or network per line, such as your district network or monitoring server. These entries are marked as coming from the console and removed again when the policy drops them; entries made locally are never touched.
  • Alerts: Set the alert email recipients.
  • Notice: Show a notice to administrators, a banner on every page of the server, such as This server is managed by District IT. Call x4000 before changing trunks.

Tick Default policy to give it to servers enrolled with a token that names no policy. A changed policy goes out at each server's next check-in.

Send commands

On the Instances tab, tick servers and choose Command n selected, or open one server and choose Send command:

  • Check for updates
  • Download an update (give the Version)
  • Approve an update (give the Version, and Install In the maintenance window or Now, when no call is in progress)
  • Refresh catalogs

Commands wait for the server's next check-in and expire after a day. Each server carries them out under its own rules.

Stop managing a server

  • On the console, Revoke refuses the server's check-ins from then on. The server removes the firewall entries and notice it took from the console; other settings stay. Once revoked, Remove deletes its history on the console.
  • On the managed server, Leave stops checking in and forgets the console. Settings the policy applied stay; firewall entries from the console are removed.

To enroll again, create a new token.

Turning the console off keeps the enrolled servers but refuses their check-ins until it is turned on again.

guides.title: Integrations: tokens and webhooks
guides.summary: Let other systems use Veyra with their own limited tokens, and tell other systems about calls, voicemail, pages and alerts with signed webhooks.
guides.html:
System → Integrations connects Veyra to the systems around it, in two directions:

  • Tokens for systems that call Veyra: a door controller that starts a lockdown page, a script that downloads the call history.
  • Webhooks for systems Veyra tells about events: a screen in the front office that shows who is calling, a ticket system that hears about alerts.

For "when this happens, do that" inside Veyra itself, without writing code, see Automation rules.

Tokens

Create a token

  1. On the Tokens tab, choose New token.
  2. Choose the Organization it belongs to. A token belongs to the organization, not to a person, so it keeps working when people leave.
  3. Give it a Name, such as Door controller, main entrance.
  4. Under Allowed to, tick only what it needs: | Allowed to | Code | |---|---| | Start pages | paging.send | | Ring bell schedules now | bells.write | | See active calls | calls.read | | Place click-to-dial calls | calls.originate | | Hang up calls in progress | calls.hangup | | Start and stop recording calls in progress | calls.record | | Read the call history | calls.history.read | | Export the call history as CSV | calls.history.export | | Read the directory | directory.read | | Run saved reports | reports.read | | Read the Prometheus metrics (server-wide; platform administrators only) | metrics.read | Tokens can never change Veyra's settings. metrics.read lets a monitoring system such as Prometheus read the server's metrics at /api/v1/metrics. The metrics are about the whole server, not one organization, so only platform administrators see this choice and can grant it.
  5. Optionally limit it with Only from these addresses (optional) (addresses or networks; empty allows any), and set when it Expires (optional).
  6. Choose Create token and copy the token now: Veyra keeps only a fingerprint and cannot show it again.

The other system sends the token as a bearer token. The window shows an example that starts a page:

curl -X POST https://pbx.example.org/api/v1/pages/<page id>/send \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Look after tokens

The list shows what each token is Allowed to do, where it may connect From, when it was Last used and from which address, and when it Expires.

  • Edit changes its name, permissions, addresses or expiry.
  • New token replaces the token. The old one stops working at once, so update the other system straight away.
  • The bin icon revokes it. It stops working at once.
Make one token per system, so you can revoke one without breaking the others.

Webhooks

Add a webhook

  1. On the Webhooks tab, choose New webhook.
  2. Give it a Name and the Address that should receive the messages, such as https://hooks.example.org/veyra. Addresses on the Veyra server itself are refused; addresses on your own network are fine.
  3. For a device on your network that has no HTTPS, tick Allow unencrypted HTTP. The message is still signed, but readable on the way.
  4. Tick the events:
    • Calls: an extension starts ringing, an extension answers a call, a finished call is in the call history
    • Voicemail: a new voicemail message is left
    • Paging: a page starts, a bell schedule rings
    • Monitoring: a monitoring alert is raised or resolved
    • Phones: a phone registers or unregisters
    • System: a configuration deployment ends Events marked live (ringing, answered) are sent once only, because a late message would be meaningless. Others are retried.
  5. Save, and copy the signing secret now. Give it to the receiving system so it can check that messages really come from Veyra.

Test and check

  • Send test sends a test message and shows the answer.
  • Deliveries lists the last 100 messages (kept for 7 days) with their result. Details shows the message and the answer; Redeliver sends one again.
  • The Status column shows OK, Failing since …, Disabled or Turned off.

A failed delivery is retried after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours and 6 hours. A webhook that keeps failing for 3 days is turned off; fix the receiver, then switch Enabled on again in its settings.

Check the signature

Each message carries a Veyra-Signature header with a time and an HMAC-SHA256 of the time and the body, made with the webhook's secret. The Checking the signature card on the page has a short example in Python. The receiver should refuse messages older than five minutes and ignore a repeated Veyra-Delivery id.

New secret creates a new signing secret. For a day, messages carry both the old and the new signature, so you have time to update the receiver.

guides.title: Automation rules
guides.summary: Make Veyra react by itself, such as emailing the office about a missed call or starting a page when a door controller calls in.
guides.html:
System → Automation holds rules of the form when something happens, if these conditions hold, do this. No programming is needed. For example:

  • A missed call to the office's number emails the office staff.
  • A door controller held open calls a secret address, and Veyra starts a page.
  • A monitoring alert emails the on-call technician.

Rules listen to the same events as webhooks, or to a request to their own address.

Create a rule

  1. Choose New rule.
  2. Give it a Name, such as Missed calls to the office. If you have several organizations, choose the Organization.
  3. When: choose what the rule listens to:
    • Calls: an extension starts ringing; an extension answers a call; a finished call is in the call history.
    • Voicemail: a new voicemail message is left.
    • Paging: a page starts; a bell schedule rings.
    • Monitoring: an alert is raised or resolved.
    • Phones: a phone registers or unregisters.
    • System: a configuration deployment ends.
    • A device calls the rule's address: the rule gets its own secret web address (see below). The trigger cannot be changed later; create another rule instead.
  4. Only if: optionally Add a condition: a Field of the event, is or contains, and a Value. The page lists the fields of the chosen event. For example, for a finished call: outcome is missed, and to.number is 5550100. All conditions must hold; text is compared without regard to capitals.
  5. Then: at least one of:
    • Email: the addresses to tell what happened. Email must be set up under System → Settings → Email delivery.
    • Start a page: a page, and the Recording to play (or The page's own recording).
  6. Quiet time (seconds) (default 60): after firing, the rule waits this long before it can fire again, so a burst of events does not page ten times.
  7. Leave Enabled on, and choose Create rule.

Rules a device can call

With A device calls the rule's address, Veyra shows the rule's address once after you create it, in a box at the top of the page. Copy it into the device (a door controller, a panic button, a script). The device sends a POST request to it; an optional JSON body becomes fields the conditions can test.

Anyone who knows the address can fire the rule, so treat it like a password. New address in the rule's window replaces it; the old one stops working.

Check that it works

  • Test now in the rule's window runs the actions within a few seconds.
  • Runs in the list shows each time the rule fired, with the result of each action.
  • The list shows each rule's State (On, Off or Last run failed with the reason) and how often it has Fired.

Delete in the rule's window removes it; for a device rule, its address stops working.

guides.title: Modules
guides.summary: Add features to Veyra with signed modules from a catalog or a package file, and enable, update, roll back or remove them.
guides.html:
Modules add features to Veyra. Open System → Module Manager. It has four tabs: Installed, Catalog, Upload and Sources.

Every module is signed by its publisher, and Veyra checks the signature before anything runs. Only modules signed by an official key run inside Veyra; each card shows a trust badge (Official, Community, Third-party or Unsigned) and Signature verified.

Install from the catalog

  1. On the Catalog tab, find the module. Latest shows the newest version that works with your Veyra; Installed shows yours.
  2. Choose Install (or Update to …). The package is checked against the catalog's checksum and the publisher's signature.
  3. Confirm with Install and enable.

If the catalog is empty, add a source on the Sources tab (see below), or wait for the daily refresh.

Upload a package

On the Upload tab, choose a .vmod file and Upload and install. It must be signed by a publisher key this server trusts. Unsigned packages are refused.

Manage installed modules

The Installed tab shows a card per module with its state, trust, version, author and health. The buttons depend on the state:

  • Install: creates its database tables and registers its permissions. It stays off until you enable it.
  • Enable: its pages and features become available to people with its permissions. Module pages appear under Modules in the menu.
  • Disable: it stops working; its data and settings are kept.
  • Settings: the module's own settings. Settings for chooses installation-wide settings or those of one organization, if the module has any.
  • Apply update: runs the new version's database changes now.
  • Roll back: goes back to the previous version.
  • Uninstall: removes it but keeps its data, so it can be reinstalled later. Tick Also delete all of this module's data to drop its data for good; you must type the module's ID to confirm. This cannot be undone.

Permissions and dependencies on each card lists what the module adds and needs.

Restart after an update

New module code runs after Veyra's services restart. When that is needed, the page shows New module code is waiting with Restart Veyra services. It takes about 10 seconds. Asterisk keeps running, so calls are not affected; the page reloads by itself.

Catalog sources

A catalog source is a signed list of modules on the web. On the Sources tab:

  • Add source: a Name and the Index address (the HTTPS address of its index.json; index.json.sig must sit next to it).
  • Check now refreshes the catalogs. They are also checked once a day.
  • The bin icon removes a source. Modules installed from it stay; they just stop getting updates from it.

A catalog is used only when it is signed by a key in /etc/veyra/trust/catalog/ on the server. Adding a trusted key is done on the server by its administrator.

When it does not work

  • Compatibility or trust problems: the card lists them, such as a module built for another Veyra version or a missing signature.
  • Last error: what went wrong the last time the module was changed.
  • This module page is not available: the module is disabled, or your role does not include its permissions.

From the server console, sudo veyra modules list lists modules, and sudo veyra modules enable <id>, disable, update, rollback and uninstall do the same as the buttons.

Writing your own module? See the module author guide.

guides.title: Your phone at a glance: My Phone
guides.summary: Turn on Do Not Disturb, forward your calls, check voicemail, call people back, keep your contacts and send a fax, all from the My Phone page.
guides.html:
My Phone is your own page in Veyra. Open it from the menu at any time. It is made of boxes called widgets: your phone's settings, your voicemail, your recent calls, your contacts and more. Your school or company chooses the starting arrangement; you can change it.

Most changes you make here take effect at once. You do not need to wait for anyone.

Your phone and call handling

The My phone widget shows your extension number, whether your desk phone is connected (Phone registered), and two cards:

Call handling

  • Do Not Disturb: callers hear busy, or your voicemail's busy greeting. Under Callers who still ring during Do Not Disturb you can list up to 20 numbers or extensions that always get through, one per line, such as your child's school or your manager.
  • Call waiting: turn it off so that, while you are on a call, other callers hear busy or go to voicemail.
  • Refuse callers who hide their number: outside callers without caller ID are turned away. Colleagues always ring.
  • Forward all calls to, Forward when busy to, Forward when unanswered to and Forward when the phone is offline to: an extension or an outside number. Leave a box empty to turn that forward off. The offline forward helps during a power or network outage.

Switches take effect as soon as you flip them; for the forwards and the list, choose Save call handling.

Find me / follow me

Rings your mobile or another phone as well as your desk phone.

  1. Choose Add a number, pick Extension or Outside number, enter it and how long it should ring.
  2. Choose whether to ring All at once or One after another, and how long your desk phone rings alone first.
  3. Outside numbers must press 1 to accept keeps your mobile's voicemail from answering the call.
  4. Choose Save follow me, then turn on Follow me.

Presence

The Presence widget sets what colleagues see next to your name: Available, Away, Busy, In a meeting, At lunch or Out of the office, with an optional short Message such as Back at 3.

  • Automatic actions… lets each state change your phone too. For example, Out of the office can turn on Do Not Disturb or forward your calls; Available can turn them off again. Choose Save actions.
  • From your calendar: connect your calendar's secret iCal address and Veyra shows you In a meeting while you have a meeting. Only the times are used; colleagues do not see your meeting titles.

Voicemail

The Voicemail widget shows your messages and greetings. See Your voicemail.

Recent calls

Recent calls lists calls to and from your phones in the last 30 days. Filter by Missed, Answered or To voicemail, and use Export for a spreadsheet file.

  • Call back calls the number for you: your desk phone rings first; pick it up and Veyra places the call.
  • Add to contacts saves an unknown number with a name.
  • Recording plays a recorded call, if your organization lets users play their own recordings.

Contacts and speed dials

Contacts holds your personal phone book. Choose New contact, then fill in a Name, a Company or place, up to 5 Numbers, an Email and Notes.

  • Favourite contacts come first. Tick Favourite in the contact, or use the button beside its name.
  • Speed dial (1–99) marks a contact for one of your phone keys.
  • Import takes lines of CSV text (name, company, number) or a file exported from here; Export downloads your contacts.
  • Call rings your desk phone first, then calls the contact.

Names from your contacts are shown on your calls and voicemail.

Colleagues

Colleagues shows who is available, on a call (red dot), or whose phone is offline, with their presence. Search by name or number, and use Call to call them through your desk phone.

Phone keys

Phone keys shows the programmable keys of your desk phone. Keys with a lock are set by your administrator and stay. Keys marked Yours are free for you: choose Set and pick:

  • Speed dial: calls a number (or one of your contacts) with one press,
  • Busy lamp: lights up while a colleague is on the phone; press it to call them or pick up their ringing call,
  • Presence: shows whether a colleague is available; press it to call.

Enter a Label on the key and choose Save key. The phone picks up the change within a minute. Clear empties the key.

Send a fax

The Conference widget lists the conference rooms your phone owns: who is in each one, with mute, remove, lock, end, recording and Invite a number. An administrator makes your phone an owner on the room's page.

The Fax widget sends a PDF as a fax, no fax machine needed.

  1. Choose Send a fax.
  2. Enter the Fax number.
  3. Choose the PDF to send: up to 20 MB and 50 pages.
  4. Tick Add a cover sheet to add a first page with To, From (left empty, it shows your name), Subject and a Note.
  5. Choose Send fax.

Your faxes lists what you sent with its state (Waiting, Dialling, Sending, Sent, Failed). You are emailed when a fax is delivered or fails. You can Cancel a fax still waiting and Retry a failed one.

Codes you can dial

Codes you can dial lists the star codes your phone accepts, for example to turn Do Not Disturb or forwarding on and off from the phone itself. Your administrator may have changed the usual codes; this widget always shows the right ones for your phone.

Arrange the page

  1. Choose Arrange.
  2. Drag a widget by its title bar, resize it from its corner, or remove it with its ×. Widgets with a lock are required by your administrators and cannot be removed.
  3. Add widget adds another, for example a second Voicemail for a shared inbox you watch. Tab adds a tab (up to 8); type in the box beside the tabs to rename the current one.
  4. Choose Save layout. Undo takes back the last change; Reset to default returns to your administrators' layout.

On a phone or a narrow window, the widgets stack in order.

If something doesn't work

  • "No phone is assigned to you": ask your administrator to assign you an extension.
  • Phone not registered: your desk phone is not connected. Check its network cable and power, or ask your administrator.
  • Call back or Call does nothing: your desk phone rings first; pick it up. Check that Do Not Disturb is off.

guides.title: Your voicemail
guides.summary: Listen to your messages from your phone or the browser, record your greetings, set an away message for the holidays, and choose your PIN.

headings.title: Away for a while: extended absence

guides.html:
When you don't answer, are on another call or have Do Not Disturb on, callers can leave you a message. Your desk phone's message lamp lights up when you have new messages. If your administrator has set it up, each new message is also emailed to you with the recording attached.

You can listen to messages from your desk phone, or in the browser on My Phone.

From your desk phone

  1. Dial *97.
  2. Enter your PIN, then press #.
  3. Press 1 to listen to your messages.

While a message plays or after it, the usual keys are: 4 previous message, 5 repeat, 6 next message, 7 delete, 9 save it to a folder. Press 0 for your mailbox options, where you record your greetings: 1 unavailable greeting, 2 busy greeting, 3 your name, 4 temporary greeting. The voice prompts tell you the keys at every step.

From another phone, dial *98, then enter your mailbox number (your extension) and your PIN.

These are Veyra's usual codes. If they do not work, check the Codes you can dial widget on My Phone; your administrator may have changed them.

In the browser

On My Phone, the Voicemail widget has two tabs.

Messages shows your messages by folder (New, Old and others). For each message:

  • Play listens in the browser.
  • Call me rings your desk phone and plays the message there, useful in a shared office.
  • Move puts it in another folder. Moving a new message to Old marks it as heard on the phone too.
  • Forward sends a copy to a colleague's box.
  • Email sends it to your email address with the recording attached. The message stays in the box unless you tick Delete it from the voicemail box once the email is sent.
  • Delete removes it.

Greetings lists your greetings, each Recorded by you or Standard (the phone system's own):

  • Unavailable: played when you do not answer.
  • Busy: played when you are on another call.
  • Name: your name, used by the directory and the standard greetings.
  • Temporary: played instead of the others while it exists. Remove it when you are back.
  • Extended absence and After hours: see below.

For each one, Record records it with your computer's microphone (up to 60 seconds; listen to it, then Save greeting), Upload takes an audio file, and Remove goes back to the standard greeting.

Away for a while: extended absence

For the summer break or a leave:

  1. Record or upload your Extended absence greeting, for example I am away until August 20. For urgent matters, call the front office at 1000.
  2. Under Extended absence, pick the First day and Last day. Leave First day empty to start now, and Last day empty to keep it on until you turn it off. Choose Save dates.
  3. Turn on Extended absence.
  4. To stop messages piling up while you are away, tick Take no messages while away: callers hear your greeting and the call ends.

On the first day, callers hear your absence greeting; after the last day, it turns itself off.

After hours

If your administrator has set office hours for your box, your After hours greeting plays instead of the unavailable one while the office is closed. A temporary greeting still takes priority.

Your PIN and greeting keys

On your account page, the Voicemail card shows where your new messages are emailed and how long your phone rings before voicemail answers.

  • Change PIN sets a new PIN of 4 to 10 digits. It starts working after your administrator's next deployment of changes, so keep using the old one until then. From a phone, the mailbox options change it at once; use 4 to 10 digits.
  • Greeting keys lets callers press a key during your greeting instead of leaving a message: Press 1 during the greeting can try your follow-me numbers or ring another number, and Press 2 during the greeting can ring another number. Say so in your greeting, for example press 1 to try my mobile.

Shared inboxes

If you watch a shared inbox, such as an attendance line, it appears as another Voicemail widget on My Phone (or add one with Arrange → Add widget), and your message lamp also lights for it. From a phone, dial *98 and enter the inbox's number and PIN. Your account page shows no Change PIN or Greeting keys for a shared inbox: its administrator sets those.

If something doesn't work

  • The PIN is refused: if you changed it recently, the old one works until the next deployment. Otherwise ask your administrator to reset it.
  • No voicemail emails: your administrator controls email delivery and the address it goes to.
  • The browser cannot record: allow the microphone for this site, or upload a recording, or record from the phone with *97.

guides.title: Your account and sign-in security
guides.summary: Change your password, set up a passkey or an authenticator app, keep your recovery codes, and sign out devices you no longer use.
guides.html:
Your account page holds your sign-in settings. Open it from the menu with your name in the top bar, or go to your account.

The Profile card shows your name, email address, how you sign in, whether two-factor authentication is on, and when you last signed in. Your name and email address are changed by an administrator.

Change your password

If you sign in with Google, Microsoft or single sign-on, you have no separate Veyra password: the page shows a Password card saying so instead of Change password. Change your password with Google, Microsoft or your organization instead.

In Change password:

  1. Enter your Current password.
  2. Enter the New password twice. It needs at least 12 characters and must not contain your name or email address. A short sentence or a few unrelated words is easiest to remember.
  3. Choose Change password.

Your other sessions are signed out, and browsers you trusted must enter the second step again.

Forgot your password? On the sign-in page, choose Forgot your password? and enter your email address; you get an email with a link to choose a new one.

Two-factor authentication

With two-factor authentication, signing in needs your password and something you have: a passkey (your fingerprint, face, device PIN or a security key) or a 6-digit code from an authenticator app on your phone. Someone who learns your password still cannot sign in.

The Two-factor authentication card says whether it is On and whether your role requires it. If it is required, set it up before the date shown, or you will not be able to sign in.

Add a passkey

  1. Choose Add a passkey.
  2. Give it a Name, for example Work laptop Touch ID.
  3. Choose Create passkey and confirm with your fingerprint, face, device PIN or security key when the browser asks. Nothing biometric leaves your device.

If the browser refuses, Veyra must be opened by its host name with a certificate your computer trusts; ask your administrator, or use an authenticator app instead.

Add an authenticator app

  1. Choose Use an authenticator app (or Add an authenticator app if two-factor is already on).
  2. Open an authenticator app on your phone (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, Authy, 1Password and others work), add an account and scan the code. If you cannot scan, choose Can't scan? Enter the key by hand.
  3. Optionally Name this device, enter the Code from the app and choose Verify and enable.

Recovery codes

When you turn on two-factor authentication, Veyra shows 10 recovery codes once. Download or copy them and keep them somewhere safe, not on your phone. Each code signs you in once if you lose your phone or security key: on the sign-in page, choose Lost your device? Use a recovery code.

The card shows how many codes are left. New codes replaces them all (your old ones stop working).

Manage your devices

Each passkey and authenticator app is listed with when it was added and last used. Rename it or remove it with the buttons on its row. Removing your only device turns two-factor authentication off. Removing a device or making new codes asks for your password again.

Trusted browsers

At the second step of signing in, you may tick Trust this browser for … days. That browser then signs you in with the password only until the date shown. The Trusted browsers card lists them: forget one you no longer use, or Forget all if a computer was lost. Changing your password also forgets them.

Active sessions

Active sessions lists everywhere you are signed in, with the Device, when you Signed in, when you were Last active, and when the session Expires. A session ends after a set time, and sooner when it is not used.

  • Sign out ends one session, for example on a shared computer you forgot to sign out of.
  • Sign out other sessions ends all of them except the one you are using.

The browser extension has its own list: see Connected apps in Use the Companion extension.

Missed-call emails

Under Missed calls, turn on Email me about missed calls to get one email for each call to your phone that nobody answered. Calls that went to voicemail send the voicemail email instead.

Voicemail

The Voicemail card lets you change your voicemail PIN and greeting keys: see Your voicemail.
